title: Is there a gene for being gay?
answer: No. Many variants each have tiny effects, and together they cannot predict a person's sexuality.
explanation: Twin and family studies show that genes play some part in same-sex sexual behaviour, alongside other influences. The largest genetic study, of about 480,000 people, found five DNA regions linked to it, and all measured variants together accounted for 8 to 25 percent of the variation. The authors stated that these results do not allow meaningful prediction of any individual's sexual behaviour.

title: Is there a gene for paedophilia?
answer: No. No gene variants have been identified, and research in this area is limited.
explanation: No DNA variants linked to paedophilia have been identified. One Finnish twin study of about 4,000 men estimated that genetic factors explained about 15 percent of differences in self-reported sexual interest in children and young people under 16, and the authors described this contribution as comparatively weak. A 2025 review of 39 biological studies, all in men, found early hormone, brain imaging and epigenetic findings, none yet established as a test.
sources: Alanko 2013, Journal of Sexual Medicine; Karanikola 2025, Frontiers in Psychiatry

title: Is there a gene for crime or violence?
answer: No. Genes play some part in antisocial behaviour, but no test predicts who will offend.
explanation: Twin and adoption studies suggest genes account for roughly 40 percent of differences in antisocial behaviour. The MAOA story began with one Dutch family carrying a rare broken copy of the gene, then a common MAOA variant that seemed to change how maltreatment affected boys; replications were mixed, though a 2014 meta-analysis supported it in males. A Finnish prisoner study naming MAOA and CDH13 has not been confirmed, and a 2022 genome-wide study of about 85,000 people found a single locus, in the FOXP2 gene.
sources: Rhee 2002, Psychological Bulletin; Brunner 1993, Science; Caspi 2002, Science; Byrd 2014, Biological Psychiatry; Tiihonen 2015, Molecular Psychiatry; Tielbeek 2022, Molecular Psychiatry

title: Are some people born to be bullies or victims?
answer: No. Twin studies find genetic influence, probably through temperament, but no specific genes are known.
explanation: In a study of 10-year-old British twins, genetic differences accounted for about 73 percent of the variation in being bullied and 61 percent in bullying others. This does not mean a bullying gene exists: genes probably act through traits such as temperament, mood and behaviour, which shape how children act and how others treat them. Polygenic scores for depression, ADHD, risk taking and body weight each relate slightly to being bullied, far too weakly to predict anything for one child.
sources: Ball 2008, Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry; Schoeler 2019, JAMA Psychiatry

title: Can my DNA predict penis size?
answer: No. Normal variation has no known genetic markers; the known genetic causes are rare conditions.
explanation: No large genome-wide study of normal penis size has been published, so there are no variants to score. A review pooling clinical measurements from up to 15,521 men found an average erect length of about 13 cm and only a modest link with height. Rare inherited conditions that disrupt male hormone production or signalling during development, such as androgen insensitivity, 5-alpha-reductase deficiency and congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, can affect genital growth, but these are medical diagnoses, not part of ordinary variation.
sources: Veale 2015, BJU International; Hughes 2012, Lancet; Imperato-McGinley 1974, Science; Boehm 2015, Nature Reviews Endocrinology

title: Is there a gene for lasting longer in bed?
answer: No. Twin studies suggest a modest genetic share, but no variant has held up.
explanation: A study of about 1,200 Finnish male twins estimated that genes explained about 28 percent of differences in premature ejaculation symptoms, though that estimate was statistically uncertain. A small Dutch study of 89 men linked a serotonin transporter variant, 5-HTTLPR, to time to ejaculation, but a larger Finnish sample of over 1,400 men found no association. No genetic test can predict sexual stamina or ejaculatory control.
sources: Jern 2007, Journal of Sexual Medicine; Janssen 2009, Journal of Sexual Medicine; Jern 2013, Archives of Sexual Behavior

title: Can my genes predict how successful or wealthy I will be?
answer: No. Scores show modest average differences in education and income, not individual outcomes.
explanation: The largest study of educational attainment, in about 3 million people, produced a score that explains 12 to 16 percent of differences in years of schooling. Only about half of that link is a direct genetic effect; the rest runs through family environment and other population effects, as comparisons between siblings show. Income scores explain 1 to 5 percent of differences in income, with only about a quarter of that direct. Most of what separates people's outcomes lies outside these scores.
sources: Okbay 2022, Nature Genetics; Howe 2022, Nature Genetics; Kweon 2025, Nature Human Behaviour

title: Is there a gene for intelligence?
answer: No. Thousands of variants each have tiny effects, and scores predict only a modest share.
explanation: Twin studies put the heritability of intelligence at around 50 percent, but it is spread across a very large number of variants. A study of about 270,000 people found 205 associated DNA regions, none of them a single 'intelligence gene'. The best scores explain up to about 11 percent of differences in test results among teenagers, and part of that shrinks when siblings are compared. A score cannot tell you a person's IQ.
sources: Plomin 2018, Nature Reviews Genetics; Savage 2018, Nature Genetics; Allegrini 2019, Molecular Psychiatry; Howe 2022, Nature Genetics

title: Is there a 'warrior gene' or a gene for my personality type?
answer: No. Single-gene personality stories mostly came from small studies that failed to replicate.
explanation: Personality traits, measured on sliding scales rather than as types, are roughly 40 percent heritable, but genome-wide studies show this is spread across many variants with tiny effects. Single-gene stories, such as MAOA as a 'warrior gene', come from an era of small candidate-gene studies, and most early gene-by-environment findings look like false positives. Retested in large samples, 18 much-studied depression genes did no better than other genes, and reported intelligence variants largely failed to replicate.
sources: Vukasovic 2015, Psychological Bulletin; Lo 2017, Nature Genetics; Duncan 2011, American Journal of Psychiatry; Border 2019, American Journal of Psychiatry; Chabris 2012, Psychological Science

title: Can my DNA tell me how long I will live?
answer: No. Lifespan is only weakly heritable, and genetic scores shift averages by a few years.
explanation: Long life runs in families, but much of that resemblance also appears between in-laws, which points to people choosing partners with similar life prospects; allowing for this, lifespan heritability was estimated at well below 10 percent. Only a few common variants replicate, most consistently near APOE and FOXO3. A score built from parents' lifespans separated the top and bottom tenths of people by about five years on average, which says little about any one person.
sources: Ruby 2018, Genetics; Deelen 2019, Nature Communications; Willcox 2008, PNAS; Timmers 2019, eLife

title: Is there a gene for musical or sporting talent?
answer: No. Both are partly heritable, but no genetic test can identify talent.
explanation: In over 10,000 Swedish twins, how much people practised music was 40 to 70 percent heritable, and the link between practice and musical ability was mostly genetic. A study of 600,000 people found 69 regions linked to keeping a beat, each with a tiny effect. The ACTN3 'sprint' variant is more common in elite sprinters, but most people carry at least one copy, so it says little about any one person. Sport genetics researchers agree that genetic tests have no role in talent identification.
sources: Mosing 2014, Psychological Science; Niarchou 2022, Nature Human Behaviour; Yang 2003, American Journal of Human Genetics; Webborn 2015, British Journal of Sports Medicine

title: Can genes show a risk of bulimia?
answer: Not yet. Anorexia has large genetic studies; bulimia has barely been studied at the DNA level.
explanation: Family and twin studies suggest bulimia is moderately heritable, with estimates from about 39 to 62 percent. Anorexia has genome-wide studies with tens of thousands of cases and several confirmed risk regions, which is why a score can be built for it, though even that score cannot diagnose anyone. As of 2021 no genome-wide study of bulimia itself had been done, and the first large study of binge eating, a core feature, reported six regions in 2026. No validated genetic score for bulimia exists yet.
sources: Bulik 2010, Biological Psychiatry; Meijsen 2025, Nature Communications; Watson 2019, Nature Genetics; Hubel 2021, International Journal of Eating Disorders; Termorshuizen 2026, Nature Mental Health
